_comment: The roads to the Moon screen's words (ui-spec.md 4.21, design.md 2.3(e)). Outside the pack, like front-pages.json: corrections reach running games. Every number on the screen comes from the rules; only words live here, and never a ranking. Roads show in this order. A road is a Moon program that lands, with the Earth-orbit tests that make its Moon flights free to open; withoutLanding lists the ones that only fly round or orbit the Moon. firsts are the goals shown as 'Firsts on the way'. MoonRoadsTest holds every lunar-expedition program of both packs to an entry.

roads.howItWorks: A mothership stays in lunar orbit; a small lander goes down and back.
for: The Saturn V lifts it all in one launch.
The most test flights, and Firsts, on the way.
against: Two craft to develop and test.
Three seats to fill on every flight.
The Saturn V is needed only for the Moon flights: start it early.
roads.historyNote: Lunar-orbit rendezvous looked the riskiest plan: a docking 380,000 km from home. John Houbolt, an engineer at NASA's Langley centre, argued it was also the lightest, since only a small lander had to go down and come back up, and he wrote over his managers' heads to make the case. NASA chose it in July 1962, and one Saturn V could launch the whole Apollo stack.

roads.howItWorks: Two launches meet in Earth orbit; the joined ship flies on to the Moon.
for: No giant rocket: two medium ones.
against: Every flight needs two launches, and both must work.
The longest landing flight, and the most parts.
roads.historyNote: In 1961 James Chamberlin's Gemini team sketched Gemini flights to the Moon, with a light lander after a design from NASA's Langley centre: little more than a platform on a rocket engine, the astronaut standing on it among the fuel tanks. Its launch mass would have been a fraction of Apollo's. NASA chose lunar-orbit rendezvous and Apollo in July 1962, and Lunar Gemini stayed on paper.

roads.howItWorks: One ship flies to the Moon, lands whole and comes back.
for: One craft, and few flights on the way.
against: Needs Nova, the biggest rocket there is.
A heavy craft to land and lift off again.
roads.historyNote: Direct ascent was the first plan: one rocket sends the whole ship, which lands tail first and takes off again for home. It needed Nova, a rocket drawn with eight F-1 engines that could send about 68 tonnes toward the Moon. Once lunar-orbit rendezvous let the Saturn V do the job, Nova was never built.

roads.howItWorks: A Soyuz orbits the Moon; one cosmonaut lands in the LK.
for: The N1 lifts it in one launch.
Soyuz heritage; many flights on the way.
against: Two craft and a docking system to develop.
The crew crosses to the lander by spacewalk.
roads.historyNote: Korolev's N1-L3 used lunar-orbit rendezvous too, with a lander for one cosmonaut, the LK, who was to cross to it from the orbiter by spacewalk. The LK flew three times without a crew in Earth orbit, in 1970 and 1971, and worked. The N1 never did: all four launches, from 1969 to 1972, failed, and no cosmonaut went to the Moon.

roads.howItWorks: One ship flies to the Moon, lands whole and comes back.
for: One craft to develop; the fewest flights.
against: The UR-700, the largest rocket of all, and a heavy rocket from the very first test flight.
roads.historyNote: Vladimir Chelomei, Korolev's rival, proposed landing directly: the UR-700 rocket would send his LK-700 to the Moon whole, to land and fly home. The government chose Korolev's N1-L3 instead, and the UR-700 and the LK-700 never left the drawing board.

withoutLanding.line: Round the Moon and home; shares Gemini's capsule with the Gemini roads.
Into lunar orbit and home; shares Gemini's capsule with the Gemini roads.
Round the Moon and home without stopping; shares no parts with the landing roads.
